Learning Objectives
Discuss the rationale for learning about aspects of molecular biology to understand
musculoskeletal tumors.
Describe the types of derangements that influence cancer biology.
Review the chromosomal translocations that are important in orthopedic oncology.

Introduction

and the subsequent behavior of cells, whether those cells are normal or neoplastic. The

into RNA, which is then translated into the proteins that affect all aspects of cell
behavior. The fields of molecular biology and cancer biology have evolved together to
elucidate the manner in which various alterations in the cell influence specific aspects of
tumor biology. Although this may be a daunting topic for clinicians because it may seem
distant from the practice of surgery, the body of knowledge that orthopedic surgeons
need to master is relatively concise.
Hallmarks of Cancer and the Difference Between Benign and
Malignant
Basically, a tumor is the result of cells dividing more than they should or at an increased rate.
Cells with a deranged biology use the same molecular tools as normal cells to regulate their
growth and behavior.
Cancer cells have several unique, specific differences in the end results of their altered biology.
A benign tumor may simply have altered cell division, but a malignant tumor has additional
alterations that have been dubbed the hallmarks of cancer:
Self-sufficiency of growth—Cancer cells achieve independence from external signals typically
by sustaining their own proliferative signaling, allowing them to grow at will.
Resisting cell death—Cancer cells evade external signals that should lead to senescence or
apoptosis.
Insensitivity to antigrowth signals—Cancer cells also resist the processes that suppress
growth. Genes that suppress growth, such as the Rb gene, are known as tumor suppressor
genes.
Limitless replicative potential—Noncancer cells typically die after a certain number of
replications. Cancer cells are capable of seemingly limitless division (immortality).
Inducing angiogenesis—To support their abnormally high metabolism, cancer cells induce
and encourage angiogenesis.
Tissue invasion and metastasis—Cancer cells can invade the basement membrane, enter
blood vessels or lymphatics, and spread to distant organs.
Evading the immune system—Recent studies have suggested that this important property of
malignant cells be added to the list of the so-called hallmarks of cancer.
Tumor Suppressor Genes

Genomic science has led to an understanding of certain genes that, if lost, grant new abilities
to certain malignancies.
These genes are called tumor suppressor genes because they inhibit cell growth if active and
lead to tumor formation if lost.
Although musculoskeletal neoplasia accounts for less than 1% of all cancer, it plays a role in
the identification of the two most important known tumor suppressor genes, Rb and p53.
Specific tumor suppressor genes that are important in orthopedic oncology include the
following:
Rb—Loss of the Rb gene is associated with development of retinoblastoma and
osteosarcoma.
p53—Loss of the p53 gene (known as Li-Fraumeni syndrome in the setting of germline loss) is
associated with various sarcomas (bone and soft tissue) and breast cancer.
p16/INK4a—Loss of P16/INK4a is associated with osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, and
melanoma.
APC—Loss of the APC gene is associated with the formation of desmoid tumors and familial
polyposis.
NF1—Loss of NF1 (causative of type 1 neurofibromatosis) is associated with the formation of
neurofibromas; however, it also is lost in other sarcomas.
EXT1/EXT2—Loss of EXT1 and/or EXT2 largely is associated with multiple hereditary exostoses
and osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma. EXT1 loss is associated with a higher burden of
disease and a greater risk for chondrosarcoma than EXT2 loss.
Chromosomal Translocations in Specific Tumors
Chromosomal translocations are an important type of genetic alteration that leads to cancer
formation.
Chromosomal translocations may produce fusion genes that result in abnormal chimeric
proteins, contributing to the derangement of a cell.
Chromosomal translocations also may bring certain genes close to enhancer or promoter
genes, leading to abnormal gene expression.
Specific chromosomal translocations are important to the biology of certain musculoskeletal
tumors, and the translocation and the resulting fusion gene are regularly tested (Table 1).


Summary
The information in this lesson represents the relatively concise body of molecular
biology knowledge that is important to orthopedic surgeons. Most importantly, advances
in molecular biology are constantly opening new doors for diagnosing, classifying, and
managing musculoskeletal tumors. For example, the recent approval of pexidartinib, a
monoclonal antibody targeting CSF1, offers a powerful new method for managing
tenosynovial giant cell tumor. As such targeted therapies become more common, they
will limit morbidity and mortality associated with tumors that are difficult to manage
surgically.
